messages.subject: Effect of iterations on significance
parts:
Hello everyone,
My question relates to the influence of the number of iterations vs the
reported statistical significance from the procD.allometry function. I've
noticed that when I change the value of "iter" the significance level
changes eg:

plethAllometry <- procD.allometry(coords~Csize, ~ Location,logsz = T,data=gdf, groups = Location*,iter=100*)

          Df       SS           MS         Rsq         F         Z
                                                                                          *Pr(>F)*
log(size)  1 0.064466 0.064466 0.27105 62.885 2.6668  *0.09091* .
Location   5 0.082136 0.016427 0.34534 16.024 2.7114  *0.09091* .
Residuals 89 0.091238 0.001025 0.38361
Total     95 0.237840

plethAllometry <- procD.allometry(coords~Csize, ~ Location,logsz = T,data=gdf, groups = Location,*iter=1000*)

                        Df  SS            MS           Rsq          F                       *Pr(>F)*
      Z
log(size)           1   0.064466  0.064466 0.27105  66.8829  6.5185  0.000999
Location            5  0.082136  0.016427 0.34534  17.0431 11.4511  0.000999
log(size):Location  5 0.01027 0.002055 0.04319   2.1317  7.6994   0.000999
Residuals          84 0.080965  0.000964 0.34042
Total              95 0.237840


I don't understand why this is happening or given that at 100 iterations the data suggest there is no significant effect of size on shape but at 1000  iterations there is a highly significant effect? What are the tradeoffs of using either approach to make conclusions about whether I have an allometric effect or not?

Cheers,
Angus

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Effect of iterations on significance
parts:
Angus,

There are 5 things worth mentioning.

1) The observed case counts as one iteration.  Therefore, if you want 1000 iterations, you should use iter = 999.
2) If you had done that with iter = 999 instead of 1000, then your P-values would equal 1/1000 = 0.001.  Instead, yours equal 1/1001 = 0.000999.  What this means is no random outcome of F equaled or exceed the observed case, except the observed case, which is one possible random outcome.
3) Using the same logic, I do not think you used 100 iterations.  I think you used 10, because 1/11 = 0.09091
4) Yes it is possible to get different P-values by varying the number of iterations.  If you used 99999 random iterations, your P-value might be 1/100000 or 2/100000, if by chance, one random event other than the observed case equaled or exceeded the observed case.  You could even get different results for rejecting the null hypothesis if you are comparing results from iterations equal to 10 to many iterations.  The alpha = 0.05 criterion is arbitrary.  The number of iterations is arbitrary.  It is possible to create a state where changing the iteration number changes the conclusion of the test.  You found such an example.
5) Theory dictates that as you increase the number of unique permutations, you converge toward the true P-value.  With this in mind, using few iterations is bad; using many is good.  CRAN forces examples to finish in mere seconds in published packages, so some of our examples use few permutations.  This should not be taken as tacit support for few permutations as a practice.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Effect of iterations on significance
parts:
Angus,

First, the number of iterations influenced your test because in one case you had an extremely low number of permutations.  Since the P-value is N >= observed / N total, where N is the number of permutations, if you choose N that is really small, then naturally you can influence the results.  I am willing to bet you will not see much difference if you used 5,000 compared to 10,000 permutations.  I believe any text on resampling procedures for testing hypotheses will confirm this truth.  Analogously, any text on sampling theory will discuss the perils of small samples and sampling error (and by nature, resampling experiments are sampling experiments).  Finally, even the Central Limit Theorem assumes that sample size must be large to make sense.  The number of permutations is the sample size in resampling experiments.  Choose a small size and bad things can happen.

For your follow up question, this is simple, yes you are right.  Your groups have considerably different allometries.  Do not correct for allometry and do not compare mean shapes.  Your data tell you that you need to compare the allometries.  There have been several recent discussions in this google group about the folly of correcting shape data.  You should check the archives if want to delve deeper.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Effect of iterations on significance
parts:
Angus,

 

As Mike’s reply makes clear, with permutation methods the observed significance level is directly tied to how many permutations one uses. One can see this from its procedural ‘empirics’ (ie, significance is calculated as # values >= observed / N), or from statistical theory.

 

And while the estimated significance level can vary somewhat with the N-iterations (and in repeated trials at the same N), theory predicts this will converge on the true significance level as the number of iterations increases. An empirical example of this is Fig. 3 of Adams and Anthony, where one sees convergence to a common significance as N-iterations increases (and decreasing variation across runs at the same N-iter).

 

Dean

parts:
Angus,

The lda function in the MASS package performs linear discriminant analysis (same as CVA).  This function normalizes discriminant functions, which distorts projection of data onto axes - something for which to be aware.  It also has a classification option.  The classify function of the RRPP package performs classification but does not calculate discriminant functions (instead relies on actual variable covariances).

The $data part of a gpagen object is ready to use for these functions.  Both functions’ help pages should show you how to set up analysis.

Best,
Mike
